This is a prototype boat simulator made in unity.

The boat is driven by physically accurate force calculations for airfoils moving through fluids like air or water. This is achieved by calculating the lift and drag forces for each airfoil on the boat: the sail, centerboard, and rudder.
The directions of these forces are either parallel to the fluid velocity (drag) or perpendicular to it (lift).

The magnitudes of these forces are calculated using the lift or drag formula. The magnitudes vary directly by the area of the airfoil and the coefficient of lift or drag, which is a function of angle of attack.

The magnitudes also vary directly by the properties of the fluid they travel in. The sail varies by the density and velocity of the apparent wind, while the centerboard forces are affected by different values set for the ocean's density and realtime apparent velocity.

The functions for the lift and drag coefficients of the airfoils are taken from empirical data, and approximated using piecewise functions to return an accurate coefficient for the state of the boat's airfoils at any direction relative to the fluid direction.

GitHub, https://github.com/EliteBAM/Unity-Fighting-Game-Framework
Dynamic framework for Unity designed to make the creation of fighting games as easy as possible for pros and non-coders alike.

The Framework replicates the traditional fighting game systems found in games like Mortal Kombat and Guilty Gear, such as old fashioned hitbox data with frame-perfect animation alignment and raw animation execution without frame blending.

My framework takes care of the boiler-plate systems necessary for creating such a fighting game, and abstracts the complexities of those systems away from the developer with a suite of custom visual tools built into Unity. The HitBox Editor, for example, is an Editor Extension that can be opened through the window tab.

The visual HitBox Editor allows the developer to scrub through animations using Unity's director timeline GUI, and add, remove, and key frame new HitBox data using my custom made HitBox Editor GUI.

This system allows the developer to visually create the data structures that store custom hitbox animation data into a custom seriablizable "FightAnimation" file, which my custom animation system built on the Unity Playables API will use to ensure frame-perfect synchronization of skeletal mesh animations and hitbox frame data. All this complexity is removed from the developer's concern.

Lastly, the developer is able to create all the characters for their fighting game roster entirely "code-free."

Character data serializable files can be created through Unity's contex menu under "Create -> Create New Character." From here, the developer is able to choose a character model, name, and define a moveset of combos tied to FightAnimations.

By dropping this data file into the base character controller, the new character will be set up with no code needed.

The Movelist defined in the datasheet is parsed by the framework's combat system, which parses it out into a "combo tree," where combo strings are translated into nodes of a tree where the root is "idle" input. Duplicate tree nodes are ignored, and the final tree contains a path from idle to each attack, where the traversal node is set to idle if commands aren't executed within the specified frame window.

GitHub, https://github.com/EliteBAM/Infinite-Procedural-Terrain-Generation/tree/main/Assets/Code, Demo, /downloads/craftmine.zip

Infinite Procedural Voxel Terrain.

I used 2D perlin noise and 2D chunking for this system.

The system uses a world manager to handle the processing of loaded chunks and the scheduling of their mesh generation into off-main-thread jobs using Unity's Job system.

Mesh data generation is handled on cpu threads using the Burst Compiler to create orders of magnitude faster mesh-gen machine code, and Unity's low-level mesh API to optimize mesh stream data handling and data-per vertex.

Mesh data is then sent to the GPU to be drawn to the screen using Unity Mesh  API calls.

I refactored the whole thing to add it to my portfolio, adding the concept of neighbor tracking and "edgeMaps" to efficiently and accurately generate mesh faces between chunk borders.

Between the burst compiler and the Jobs system, the chunks load extremely fast, about 0.3ms per chunk, allowing for up to a 4096-chunk render area, with 64 chunk updates per world render update before any stutter is noticed on my mobile 10980HK.

Next steps would be to add trees, which would be easy due to the neighbor system, and to parallelize the off-main-thread jobs for even more performance and simultaneous chunk loading.

Of note: The Unity Mesh.ApplyAndDisposeWritableMeshData() call is a current "bottleneck," as it is the only way to apply the mesh data generated in the jobs, and it is impossible to call without locking the main thread. This inevitably causes a hitch when loading copious data. In the future I'd like to refactor the world manager to support staggering this call over multiple frames, giving a huge smoothness on world updates, allowing for even immensely greater render distances and more complex chunks.

I built a raytracer in JavaScript, integrated in an Electron environment with Vite (hi Bitshift! I made this one for you guys). I made this project to gain implementation experience with raytracers from the ground up while also priming my JavaScript skills.

I decided to code the project in "prototypes-with-constructor-functions" syntax because I found it interesting and different from my usual Java / C# background.

I implemented matrices, vectors, points, rays, and all the associated math functions between them from scratch.

I implemented sphere rendering for now using sphere intersection calculations.

I then implemented the main render function, which follows a phong lighting model.

The renderer is currently offline, but I’m excited at the idea of GPU accelerating it with WebGPU just for fun! I already wrote all the data structures to use performant data types, and it’s quite fun having a JS renderer running as its own Electron app!

Original art, animations, and code. Developed in Unity.

Inspired by the third person combat of Dark Souls.

Integrates third-person camera with a third-person melee conbat system. The system gives the player a light attack and a heavy attack mode. There are two animations for each mode that seamlessly blend with each other. Heavy and light attacks and also blend together in a combo. 

Each attack has an "active frame" attack window using unity Animation Event toggles. This gives each attack the structure of "wind-up," "attack," and "recovery." During "wind-up," the player's direction is controllable with both keyboard and mouse, creating a responsive and natural game feel.

The player is also equipped with a sprint and dodge roll.

See video for a full demo.

This project represents a completed baseball batting training program built in Unity.

The main structure of the program can be described as four systems running in parallel: 
- the player input system
- the pitch generation system
- the baseball force simulation system
- the bat collision detection system. 

These four systems run continuously throughout the program’s operation and continuously pass relevant output data to each other in order for them to operate. The player input system continually gathers sensory input data from the virtual reality apparatus, which is used to update the position and rotation of the player camera and the virtual baseball bat. The player input system also continually outputs relevant position data to be continuously interpreted by the bat collision system. In parallel, the pitch generation system manages a timer and generates a new baseball pitch with unique parameters once that timer reaches zero. The pitch generation system repeats this process continuously and passes on the pitch parameter data to the baseball force simulation system with each pitch generation. Once a pitch has been generated, the baseball force simulation system uses those pitch parameters to continuously simulate the magnus effect and other relevant forces throughout the lifetime of the ball’s trajectory until it collides with an object. It is this relationship that defines the general process of this program.

The training program implements physical forces that are not typically accounted for in Unity. 

For example, rotational forces and forces generated by differences in air pressure that play a key role in defining the curved trajectory of baseballs as they fly through the air were not normally taken into consideration in Unity’s default simulation. To solve this problem, I implemented a calculation of forces that are caused by what is known as the Magnus effect into the already existing Unity system in order to produce different baseball pitches that had not only realistic behaviors, but that could also be thrown for strikes.

Above is a demo of the custom controller designed to be used with the Virtual Reality headset.

The controller sends sensory data from a 9 degree of freedom sensor back to the simulation, where it is then processed to articulate the virtual baseball bat in the simulation.

Using this controller, the player gets the realistic feel of holding a baseball bat, further enhancing the accuracy of the training simulation.

Though out of the scope for this project, future developments of this training program could include the following enhancements:

1. Implementing motion capture data for the pitcher for more accurate pitch telegraphing.
2. Implementing a PBR rendering workflow, using realistic custom Unity materials to give depth to the scene.
3. Implementing a custom shader for realistic field grass, made in either Unity HLSL or Unity's Shader Graph.

This is a prototype for a procedural world generator that generates discrete sized worlds.

The intended use was for generating a tile-based world for a 2D top-down survival game.
Refine world resolution, size, and "feel" with auto-updating perlin noise settings.
Perlin clamping levels can be adjusted to modify the water level, beach size, and overall landmass size.

Voronoi noise is used to generate a biome map. Biomes can be added on the fly. Voronoi settings can be modified to change the number / size of biome groups, as well as the distance function used to classify a cell's biome. Traditional distance gives straight, harsh cutoffs, while Minkowski's distance formula yields cool twisty borders between biomes.
Biomes can also be created in a serialized generation profile. Profiles can be swapped on the fly to generate worlds or levels of different varieties.
